utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have a cite, please, from the book you were reading from yesterday when you were reciting what the book said about a conversation between the NATO pilot and a controller. Open it, please, at the page of the conversation and hand it to me. Page 86.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you also hand me, please -- I don't know if it's been made to produce it, but I'd like to see the leaflet that you've produced that I think you were suggesting was dropped by a plane. It was in a plastic cover.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have even more than that, Mr. Nice. I have lots of things. I don't know which one you're interested in. I think it was this strategic bomber B52.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... produced yesterday, please. So if you just hand me the one you showed.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to show them all to you, but I haven't been allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the conversation allegedly recorded and set out in the book, have you ever heard that audiotape yourself, if it exists?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it's not "allegedly recorded." It's been recorded. I even heard the audiotape. And by the way, it was broadcasted on various media, including, I believe, by your radio stations. And only after that Jamie Shea was forced to admit that it was NATO planes who targeted the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... have you brought a recording with you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't brought the recording with me, but I can get hold of it and make it available subsequently, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... check what you've read out from the book, please. Where can we --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you. You can get hold of it, in addition to official documents that are certainly available in the military archives, you can get it from Radio Television Belgrade, from CNN, BBC. Any serious broadcasting agency. Your contact will be able to give you the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And by the way, you can get it from the command of the NATO forces, if they are willing to give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... return to this topic if I think it justifies the time later. As to records, contemporaneous records, this: When you responded to the Commission for Cooperation, what contemporaneous, what originally contemporaneous records did you have to refer to, if any?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're asking me about the occasions when I gave statements to the commission, what relevant documents I had available to me. Well, that depends on the activity the statement concentrated on. When I gave a statement about the activity of my unit and its involvement in the anti-terrorist action in the broader area of Orahovac, which in principle includes Celine, by that time I had a couple of documents from that period; namely, the order of the brigade commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you. I had the order of the brigade commander for the anti-terrorist action. I had his original decision map, and I had his subsequent analysis that he prepared after the anti-terrorist action. I believe some of these documents have been introduced here, and I have all three of them; the order, the map - or, rather, the decision - and the analysis. They are numbers 3, 4 and 5 in my set.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from the map and the order, what other documents did you have available to you to refer to when preparing the statements for the VJ commission?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a commission of the army of Yugoslavia. It was a Commission for Cooperation with the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. As for that period, I only had these three documents, as I've said. And of course I had what every man has, my own memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And even before I received this task, I spoke to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice perhaps you can assist on this. My understanding was that it was a commission established by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Albeit the membership wasn't military but much wider than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The evidence we've had was that it was set up by one of the ministers who organised the particular Commission for Cooperation with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this particular commission, you say, wasn't confined to military evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents we have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents we have, to some of which reference has been made, that it was established, indeed, by the Ministry of the Defence in April of 2001, and insofar as I can find the first original document from our file on this, it's been translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not necessary to resolve this just now, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I'll find the earliest title, but there's never really been any doubt that it's a VJ body - I'll deal with it as necessary with this witness - which came between the National Council for Cooperation and the army for the purpose of the provision of material by those in the army or by the army itself, but I'll get the original documents for the best description that we can in the most economic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I'm only concerned to know what documents you had available to you when you made your statements to the -- or for the commission. You've referred to the two documents from Delic and the one map. Do I take it that you did not have access to your daily records, subsequently called -- or daily reports, subsequently called combat reports?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I had two documents. I said I had had three; namely, the order, the decision on the map, and third, the analysis, the estimate of the anti-terrorist action. Furthermore, what you're talking about are not my notes. Those were documents prepared by the unit, but I don't have them because they stayed in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received them about month --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... listen to the questions. Just give you an example. Take your time because we want to save your time. I asked you if, apart from two documents and one map, you had access to your daily combat reports or daily reports. The answer is no, you didn't have access to them; correct? That's all you needed to say.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you ask me such a specific question, you have received a specific answer. Look at the transcript. You just said that I had said that I had two documents, Delic's documents. It's the document of the brigade commander. It's not Delic's document. And my answer would be that at that time I certainly did not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm going to make them much simpler for you, because I suspect you're wasting time, or suggest you're wasting time, but if you find them difficult ... Now, listen to this question: When you made your statements to the VJ commission, did you have the war diary of your unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the war diary of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't think you understand my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have the war diary of your commander, Delic's, brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're obviously not listening to me. The only three documents that I had I enumerated for you. If I tell you that they were the only three documents, that means I didn't have any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are to answer the question that has been asked. The question is did you have the war diary of your commander, Delic's, brigade? What's the answer; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many statements did you make in the course of your dealings with the commission?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be precise about that, but it was from ten to 15 statements, with a proviso that two statements were given for -- or, rather, concerning the area of Korenica, and the other statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of eight, I think. Do you have all the ten to 15 with you so that we can discover what are the other statements you've made that haven't been provided to us?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the only thing that's missing is my statement concerning Brestovac, Randubrava, and the other statements are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have those other statements in your possession today so that I can read them or have them read?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Nice. I do have my statements. And I also have the statements of my subordinates whom you did not allow me to mention. They are some of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- officers who were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you're making a lot of commentary in the course of your answers. Can you explain why you say I didn't allow you to refer to the statements of your subordinates? We haven't reached that yet. Why did you say I didn't allow you to refer to the statements your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that you did not allow me. I said that I had not been allowed to do that. It all depends on the interpretation you're getting, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm told that your language was quite specific. You sought to lay the blame at me, at my door, and this characterises your evidence. You're an extremely partial witness, Mr. Vukovic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, the witness explains that he did not say that you prevented him. He said that he was prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have the advantage of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It may have been a matter of translation. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are you aware of an operation known as Grabez?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of an operation, whatever it may have been named, organised by Farkas to deal with army officers who it was thought were out of line, acting out of line?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If you mean Geza Farkas, I know him personally, but I have never had any professional contact with him during my entire service. As for the action you are referring to, I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know about the order issued by my immediate superior concerning discipline and concerning all incidents of violation of that discipline --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- by the units. I have some of those orders here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any other Colonel Dragan Vukovic who was serving in Kosovo, to your knowledge, in 1999, or are you the only one by that name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This witness, I believe, is Vlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you the only one?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you're asking me now. Are you asking me about 1999, 1992, Dragan Vukovic or Vlatko Vukovic? Could you be precise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vlatko. Are you the only one?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, Mr. Nice. This surname is rather common in my country. I cannot answer you with either a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the first name as well? The first name Vlatko, is that also common?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there is another officer with the same name and surname in the army of Yugoslavia, but as far as I know, he is a traffic officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is also a colonel, even older than I am, and I believe he got his rank of colonel earlier than I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, that was a simple answer to the question, and but for Judge Robinson's intervention, that answer would not have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to look, please, at a visual aid that we've used before. I'll just distribute this, please. Copies, again, available for the overhead projector. Now, I'll explain what this is. Take your time to look at it. Of course it's in English, but since it's nearly just names, this is a visual aid that shows for various locations where there is material suggesting that on particular days the VJ was involved in committing offences. So just to explain it to you, if we take one example and then I'll ask you the question I want to ask you. Can you see at the top -- Djakovica will do. You see Djakovica, top left-hand side, and there's a big square box pointing down towards Djakovica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether the witness can follow this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see, I see. I can see well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what the box suggests is that for this particular town there are various sources of information; Paddy Ashdown, a witness called K32, a book under "Under Orders," a number of witnesses, the book called "As Seen, As Told," further witnesses, a further passage from the book, and so on. So that that box suggests that for Djakovica there are various sources of information about the VJ. That's what the visual aid is about. Now, I want you to tell us the following: For which of the various named places - and we'll go through them in a minute - for which of the various named places are you actually able to give us direct evidence of what happened? Not evidence that you'd heard from other people but direct evidence. So if we start in the middle of the map and we look at Velika Krusa, just yes or no, are you able to tell us what happened from your own knowledge, what happened at Velika Krusa between the 24th and 27th of March? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us directly what happened at Perane [phoen], 25th to the 30th of March, from your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean -- do you mean Pirane?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going round, we see in the same general area Nogavac between March and April. Do you have direct knowledge of Nogavac?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the 25th to the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Trnje, on the 25th of March. Do you have direct knowledge of Trnje?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have direct knowledge of Mamusa on either the 25th of March or the 27th of March?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Mamusa's concerned, I have direct knowledge about the 27th, 28th of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the same general --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- area, Lesane, on the 28th of March. Do you have direct knowledge of that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find that place. I don't think that place exists in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... but if you don't know about it, then the answer is obviously that you don't have direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's east of Trnje, I don't know for certain --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I haven't been east of Trnje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, do you have direct knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bela Crkva on the 25th of March. Do you have direct knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving north, do you claim to have direct knowledge of events in Djakovica itself at any time between June 1998 and April 1999? Do you have direct knowledge of what happened in Djakovica within those periods?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the town of Djakovica itself, I have direct knowledge only about the night of the 24th of March, which is when my barracks was targeted as well as the residential civilian part of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Meja. Do you have direct knowledge of what happened in Meja on the 27th and 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have knowledge about Meja for the 27th and the 28th of April but also the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if we look a little further afield to -- and this is simply to discover the limits of your asserted knowledge. If we look, for example, to places like Studencani or Rastani to the north-east of the area we've been looking at, is that too far away for you to have direct knowledge, or do you claim direct knowledge of what happened in those places?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any direct knowledge. I only know of what I heard through communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pusto Selo or Orahovac. Do you have any direct knowledge of what happened in those places in March of 1999 for Pusto Selo or in April -- or in 1998 or March of 1999 for Orahovac? Do you have direct knowledge of either of those places?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pusto Selo, that's where part of my unit was in September 1998. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Later on, I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Orahovac when the anti-terrorist action was taking place in Senovac, Drenovac, Pusto Selo. That's where I was, in Orahovac. That's where we set out from. And I passed through Orahovac a few other times when we were carrying out anti-terrorist actions, but I don't have any concrete knowledge about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, looking at the places slightly further to the south. For example, Landovica. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Landovica, no. I wasn't in Landovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Korisa?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know about Korisa is what I heard and what I read in books.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we've identified the limits. I shan't necessarily ask about all those towns but we now know the geographical limits of the witness's understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, the best records, written records of what happened at the time are which records? That's what I want to know the answer to. Is it the daily reports or combat reports and the war diaries? Are those the best records to tell us what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not the best way, it's the only way to record what happened. So these are all kinds of written documents. With your permission, I would like to say that you've given me a map that I don't know how to read, but I see what your sources of information are. I know a lot of these people. Well, not a lot. I know one man, and I can tell you that your sources are extremely good. I even see here a colleague of mine. If I'm reading this correctly, it's Nik Peraj. I know him personally and I can say quite a few things about him. I also see here that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have you asked a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just refrain from these comments, and listen to the questions and answer them and we'll get along much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness now please have not the extracted version of his daily reports, which are tab 2 in the binder, but the full version that was subsequently provided. Now, this is a document that it's been almost impossible to read. Of course, one makes no complaint about difficulties with handwriting but that's just a reality. If we can lay a copy on the overhead projector as well. We'll have to then, I'm afraid, do our best with the one copy on the overhead projector. Does the Court have copies of the full volume?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been provided by the Defence but apparently not in adequate numbers. I hadn't appreciated that. And it's a very substantial document. Mr. Nort, you'll see on the top right-hand corner of these pages, numbers, and, and if we go, please, to -- one minute. Page -- I think it's page 99 or thereabouts on the top right-hand corner. No, it's later than that. Sorry. No. Could you go to page 126 in the top right-hand corner. Your Honours, we do have some translations of this limited portion and I'll make those available when Mr. Nort has found page 126 and the witness can start looking at that to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Now, if you can look at those pages, please, Mr. Vukovic. And if Mr. Nort or someone could kindly distribute the translations we have. What we can see on the screen at the moment is the 24th of March, apparently. It's just about visible on the screen, middle of the right-hand side. And the translations coming to the Court show, and perhaps you'd be good enough to confirm, that under item number 1, if you'd follow it, please, it says as follows: "In the zone of responsibility of the -- of 2/549th Motorised Brigade, the activities and movements of Siptar terrorist forces were not noticed." Now, this is a record from your unit, so no alleged terrorist force activity noticed; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written in paragraph 1, but you have to read the entire report so that it would be clear to you. You cannot take things out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please read paragraph 3 as well, and then it will be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, would you now please go to the bottom of the page and read paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Armed aggression carried out by NATO --" just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let me read it for you because we've had it translated. "Armed aggression has been carried out by NATO forces through synchronised attacks on the border of the Republic of Albania which they have marked the Republic of Albania border lengthwise throughout the mountains." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the border of the Republic of Albania, the rim of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do, please, with the topic I was asking you about, which was the movement of Siptar alleged terrorist forces in your immediate area of activity? It doesn't, does it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the zone of responsibility of my battalion, no armed terrorists were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, these fires were in Albania or, rather, these lights were in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please, Mr. Nort, and the top entry, number 5 reads: "Civilian people in the surrounding areas and in the zone of operation of --" your unit -- "of the 549th Motorised Brigade, behaved satisfactorily." Item 4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I read it out and I asked the witness to agree. He hasn't replied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that what item 4 says: Civilian people in the surrounding areas of your zone behaved satisfactorily?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says in item 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, trying to make sense of this document for the very, very important period, we must spend a minute or so, because the next relevant entry at 5.3 is a little curious because it reads, does it not: Day 26th of March - so we were on the 24th and it's now an entry for day 26th of March - "The 2nd unit of the 549th Motorised Brigade in terms of lengthwise security of the DG was engaged in a way as follows ..." and then it says: "Drina Patrol ... Ambush ... Ambush ... Ambush." So my first inquiry is can you explain how we move straight from the 24th of March in a contemporaneous document at sequential paragraph number 5.3 to an entry for the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, if you look at paragraph 5, it says: "Activities and the situation within the unit." And then in subparagraphs 5.1 and 5.2, reference is made to what will be done on that day. According to the orders from 1998, we were duty-bound to submit a day or two in advance a proposal to our superior command in order to engage a unit. Could you please let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this going to explain why we've got an entry for the 26th of March, and let me just complete the problem because it's one that you may be able to answer to us: If you go down to 5.5, you'll see we come back to the 25th of March, and then if you go to the right-hand side of the page, if Mr. Nort will be good enough to display it for us, we see that there's another entry there on the right-hand side, just underneath the stamp for 25th of March. So that the sequence of dates appears to be, but you may be able to explain it for us and I just want your help: 24, 26, 25, 25. Can you explain how this sequence of dates comes about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 127 is the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the mention of the 26th of March on the previous page, I've already told you the reason during my testimony. Any engagement of a unit has to be proposed beforehand, and that is what it says in point 5.3: "On the 26th of March, 1999, the 2nd battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade in terms of lengthwise --" or, rather, "in-depth security of the state border will be engaged in the following way ..." or "as follows..." So that is what we envisage, how we are going to engage it. If the command of the brigade does not allow it, then they will say, "No, don't do it that way, engage them this way," and that has to be done two days in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why does the entry for the 25th come after the entry for the 26th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's been explained. It's a mistranslation on the face of it, because the translation we have in English is "was engaged," and the witness has quite plainly said "will be engaged," and before doing that, said that this is a plan that had to be submitted two days in advance of being carried out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you let the witness read the B/C/S and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy because I want to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That explains the 26th, which I hope might well be the case. Then we come, at 5.5, to the 25th, the entry for the 25th.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this previous report, I assume, was sent out at 1600 hours, because we were still sending -- rather, I'm sorry, 1700 hours, concerning the situation as it was at 1600 hours. Later on that was changed and the brigade command had given us orders to send a report at 1300 hours concerning the situation as it was at 1200 hours so that they could observe what they had to do vis-a-vis the corps command. However, since the 25th of March, after the report was sent about the 24th, it had to be written this way. You see what it says here. At 0225 hours, the last unit left the premises. He has to send information as to what was done between one situation as it was described in one telegram and the other situation as described in the other telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, let me explain my position here. I can follow this evidence very clearly if you answer the questions that are asked. As soon as you go off on a frolic of your own, deciding what you will and will not tell us about, then you simply cause confusion. You do no good to anyone's case. Please, for my benefit, listen to the questions you've been asked and answer them. And the question you were asked was about the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about letting the witness just read the 5.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd just read 5.5 for us, please, or the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5 is activities in the unit, and 5.5 is: "On the 25th of March at 0225 hours, in the region of the village of Brekovac on the road between Logas Poprastori [phoen] Djakovica, a motor vehicle TAM 130, T10 was overturned, Deutz, registration number K 6061, from the anti-armour rocket platoon. The driver was Milosavljevic Slobodan. The assistant driver was soldier Dimic Goran, who was at that place instead of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... thank you very much. Now, if we just acquaint the Judges with the format of the next two pages. Mr. Nort, we can see that there's on the left-hand side -- that's it, then on the right-hand side we've looked at once before but the witness says it's the 26th of March. I'm quite prepared to accept that it may be the 26th of March. It looks a bit like it. And then if you'd take us to the next page, please, we see the continuation of an entry on the left, and then on the right we see the 27th of March. There's not very much writing but it's -- And then the next page, we come to the 28th of March on the left-hand side. We've got the 28th of March on the left-hand side of page 129. It's a bit -- I think it's a bit further up than that, probably. Just to see it. That's it, thank you for finding it. And then on the right, perhaps you noticed this, and just help us with this, Mr. Vukovic: We can see on this page the 28th of March, and then on the right-hand side you can see we come directly to the 3rd of April, so that there would appear to be some days missing between the 28th of March and the 3rd of April. So a first and simple question is: Can you explain why there are no entries in the daily reports for the 28th of March to the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already explained that in part, that quite a bit of documentation, and there were quite a few of such reports for 1998 and 1999, were destroyed either when my barracks were hit or the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all fairness, at that time I was not at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, this document has been presented to us as a continuous record with sequential page numbers written in in the top right-hand corner; 128, 129. The entries on the page that we're concerned with, 129, would appear to be continuous because the last entry on the left-hand side, if Mr. Nort could show it to us, is numbered 8 under the date of the 28th of March, and at the top right-hand part of page 129, the number is 9. So this would appear to be a continuous record. Can you explain to us, please, how this record does not contain entries for the days 29th, 30th, 31st of March and 1st and 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only explanation that I have, and which seems quite plausible to me, and after all that's what I said to the lawyer because he put the same question to me when he showed me this document, was that my command post had been hit, that there was relocation, that I personally was not at the command post. I joined up with my unit only on the 3rd in the afternoon. Communications were not functioning because the communications centre in Djakovica had been hit, and probably for those reason the report did not go through communications. It is possible, and I'm sure of that, that the report was sent through a messenger, that a messenger took a motor vehicle and took it to the brigade command, took the report to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... promised His Honour Judge Bonomy we wouldn't ask you to go through evidence. It's simply for reasons of legibility. For these pages, I want you to do something for us, please. It shouldn't take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, you could go back to page 127, and if the witness could have that. And then we'll do the same for the other two pages. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look through these entries - take your time and go through them - and draw to our attention anything on any of these entries that gives an account of the actions of your unit or of any other unit in Bela Crkva, Celine, Velika Krusa, or any of those other places in that area that you've been telling us about. Do you understand my request? That you should read through it yourself, silently, don't read it all out loud, but draw to our attention anything that amounts to information of what happened at Bela Crkva, Celine, Velika Krusa, and so on. So start on page 127, start on the 25th or the 26th, and tell us what you find.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What can be seen here are two pieces of information. One is precisely 5.5, because as the unit went out to complete its task, one motor vehicle was overturned. And then please find item 8, the last bullet. It says: "The execution of the task according to document number 1278-2, dated the 23rd of March, 1999." Mr. Nice, that is precisely the order of the brigade for this anti-terrorist operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, if I understand the question correctly, you are being asked to go through the documents and see whether there is anything, any information that happened at Bela Crkva, Celine, Velika Krusa, and so on. So you are simply to go through the document and tell us whether you see any reference to any of these names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Nowhere in these documents, I'm sure of that, is there any mention of that except for the war diary. There is an addition for the 26th -- for the 25th and the 26th, rather, because that was the activity of the unit. And this is a document that is written at the command post. Part of the unit that was engaged in Bela Crkva and Celine was not at Zub where this was being written, so my deputy could not write things off-the-cuff what we did 25 or 30 kilometres away from him. There was no need to write it down here, because the commander of the brigade was in the field all the time. So what was the point of writing a report when he can see what is going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you're saying that you're quite sure that neither of these pages, none of these pages, will have anything to do with the topic in which we're interested then we'll move on to something else but I certainly want you to have the chance -- I don't want to have to suddenly face in re-examination some suggestion that some part of these documents that we can't, I'm afraid, read relate to these topics. Are you quite sure that Bela Crkva, Celine, Velika Krusa, and so on are not referred to in any way on pages 127, 128, and 129? Are you quite sure about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That leaves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Nice. Sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we get the answer from the witness when the item 5.5 had been written? I'm still confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help His Honour Judge Kwon, please. The item 5.5, was it written on the 25th or was it written in advance of the 25th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is it under 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not under the 24th. It is under the 25th. At least, in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think what His Honour has in mind, and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, if you go to the previous page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us see the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- sequential numbering for the 24th starts with whatever it is, number 1, and runs through a sequence of numbers, and lo and behold, 5.5 is part of that same sequence of numbers which would seem to be connected with the entries for the 24th, but it refers to the 25th. The entry for the 25th doesn't look like the start of a new day's entry, you see? I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think that's His Honour's concern.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the date is the 24th, but let me just remind you that this is a report from the 24th. That does not mean that it was sent on the 24th, because I said that during the night of the 24th the first thing that was hit was the stationary communications centre in the barracks of Devet Jugovica, and it is certain that this report was sent later and written later, but indeed it was registered under this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that satisfies Your Honour, but I wasn't going to take any more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could read 5.3 again for clarity. 5.3 on the day of 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the 26th of March, actually. "On the 26th of March, 1999, the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade providing security in-depth of the state border, we shall be engaged or will be engaged in the following way: Drina --" that is a coded name on the map, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That, therefore, leaves us as -- because there's nothing in this document about what happened at the places in which we are interested, Bela Crkva and so on, it leaves us with the war diaries as the only available contemporaneous written records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only document of mine, with the exception of the three documents from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you'll recall that in light of the witness's health problems, we're going to sit at one-hour intervals and take 15-minute breaks. So we will adjourn now for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what year or years did you make your statements to the commission, please?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements to the commission I made in January 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All on the same occasion, roughly? I mean, I'm not suggesting you made them all on the same day, but you just had one visit to the commission and you made them all in January 2003, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Djurovic told me what dates I was to address, or I wrote the statements at home and I needed three or four days, I can't say exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine. They were all made at one session, effectively one session. Tell us, please, about the role that the book --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- "As Seen, As Told" played in Colonel Djurovic's inquiries and your responses.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions by Colonel Djurovic, well, they -- it did not play any role because I saw the book for the first time sometime at the end of 2001, beginning of 2002. I took it and photocopied the portions related to the areas and zones where my unit spent time. And once again, it played no role in my answers because I have my own opinions about the book. If you would like to hear them, I shall be happy to give them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll turn to that book in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You explained to us that the expert body of the commission served the function of sorting out problems of interpretation where there were different interpretations of events. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that that was raised. So certain events had to be explained for which we can say that there were different interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So tell us then, please, how did the commission and its expert report deal with different interpretations of events? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the expert -- it wasn't up to the expert team to deal with the problem of different interpretations. As far as I understood it, it was supposed to take the statements of the actors, the people involved, and to send them to the commission. And as far as I know, the commission, through the ministries -- now I can't be quite certain whether it was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs or whether that's the ministry -- whether that ministry sent it on to the International Tribunal. I think the commission didn't process the statements at all of the people that provided them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was your answer, you see. You volunteered it to the accused. What conceivable function could a commission of -- a committee of experts, part of this commission, have in resolving differences in interpretation? That's why I wanted you to help us. What did they do?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you what they did exactly because I wasn't a member of that expert team. All I can do is guess or speculate, and that wouldn't be in order for this time or this place. I know that they asked me to provide a statement. I provided them with a statement. What they did with that statement I really didn't ask them nor was I interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... would be that the commission's concern was that everybody should give the same account and in that way resolve what you described as differences of interpretation. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say. I don't agree with that position of yours. I think quite the reverse was true and that it was exclusively the goal and object of this exercise was to arrive at the truth, and there can only be one truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help me, then, please, with this: If that's the object, getting the evidence before the Tribunal, why not simply provide all the raw material, like the diaries, the daily records, the daily combat reports? Wouldn't that be the best material to provide to a court trying to inquire into these matters?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, Mr. Nice. However, I know that you have a problem with translation, even of the excerpts that we send in of the most characteristic reports. But you keep on asking me about the work of the Commission for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal, and I can't help you there because I never attended the work of that commission. I never took part in its work. And I personally think that you have very many documents at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll turn to one of the documents that we've been looking at. It's in the Delic file. It's 356. While it is coming to you, as a soldier in the course of combat -- as a soldier in conflict, you would -- in a conflict, you would recognise, would you not, that there has to be a civilian control for military activities. Were you aware at your level what was the civilian control, political control, of military activities?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to say something about that yesterday, but I was not allowed to do so. In war and peace, it is the president of the republic who commands the army, once again pursuant to decisions made by the Supreme Defence Council, which is a civilian structure, conditionally speaking, of course. It is a constitutional category, and this went down to the law on the army, the law on the rules of service and the direct documents on the basis of which commanding officers function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did -- did you understand that in the Kosovo conflict the president of the republic was operating, for military purposes, through sittings of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During the conflict in Kosovo, from March 1999 until June, did you understand that the process you've just described was in effect, that the president was operating through the Supreme Defence Council in instructing the military what to do?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is quite normal that at the Supreme Defence Council the most important questions linked to the army are discussed and that instructions are given, directives given, guidelines given for the deployment of the units. Later on, the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia elaborates on the orders given and sends them down the chain of command to the units in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anybody suggest to you at any stage or did it ever get talked about at any stage that there was a different form of political control other than the political control that tracks back to the president?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I don't understand what you're asking me. I never dealt in politics, so it's all alien to me as a soldier, so alien that I can't answer it. I don't actually understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to agree with the witness. That question was not precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please, at this document, which is tab 356 from Delic. You'll be given the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if Mr. Nort would display it on the overhead projector. You'll see that this is a document coming from something called the Joint Command. Were you aware of the existence of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the existence of this term "the Joint Command," I heard that for the first time during the preparatory phase here when I was handed this document, which is here and is number 2 in my files.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we go to paragraph 5 of this document, we see an order not coming directly to your unit, of course, but going to Delic, which says under paragraph 5 -- and if you've got that on the overhead projector, please. Couple of pages on, paragraph 5. We see that amongst the instructions being given by the Joint Command at the time was -- paragraph 5, please, Mr. Nort. Page 3. We see an instruction being given in the clearest terms to break up and destroy the STS in the following areas: Celine, Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa, et cetera, continue the attack, destroy the remaining STS in the axes of attack, and the next task is to break through along the following lines, and then it gives the villages of Mala Krusa, Nogavac, and so on. If you go to the previous paragraph - I should have taken to you the previous paragraph - under "Task," it sets out that in a joint action with the MUP, to carry out an attack from the all-round support point on the following axes, and then it mentions the villages of Bela Crkva, Mala Hoca, Velika Krusa, and so on. So this order is consistent, is it not, with the order that you received, you say, from General Delic. Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is consistent, but here it doesn't say together with the MUP forces here. It says decision. This is a classical order by the corps commander, and he says, "I have hereby decided that the MUP forces should be supported in executing their attack." So he's just supporting the forces of the Ministry of the Interior and not issuing tasks to the units of MUP themselves. And if you read this in detail, but you will have to read it in detail, the entire document in detail, in fact, for it to be clear to you. Don't extract portions from the whole and out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, just answer the questions, please. You have --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to give you advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'd ask the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for you to give advice to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- to observe the dignity of this Court and not to let the witness run away with himself. Could we have Exhibit tab 357, which is another of the documents that the witness has referred to. This is the order coming from Delic. And just to remind the Court, although I think it will be in everybody's mind, if we go to paragraph 4 of this order, which is on page 2 and over on page 3, Mr. Nort, actually. We see a reference to cut off and destroy the STS in the general sector of the village of Retimlje. And then over the page, with axes identified as Bela Crkva and Nogavac. Then if we go -- and reference to routing and destroying the STS along that axis. And if, Mr. Nort, if you'd take us, please, to paragraph 5.5, and I know this is in everybody's mind, but we'll just remind ourselves of it. At 5.5, the assignment given to your unit was to carry out an energetic attack and search the village of Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, that was the order you originally received; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the order by the commander that I -- brigade commander that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Remind the Chamber and yourself of the nature of the allegations about Bela Crkva. It's an admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd just take this photograph, please, Mr. Nort. It's from - thank you very much - Exhibit 157, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is the railway bridge covering the stream that leads from Bela Crkva in the direction of Rogovo. Are you familiar with this location?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise this photograph because I never went in a train that way. I just went along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I can't be of assistance to you and tell you whether it is indeed the bridge that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another photograph from the same exhibit, again just to remind the Chamber. And if Mr. Nort would -- that point there. Thank you very much. If you look at this, the evidence is that this is indeed Bela Crkva, that Mr. Nort's going to point out where the stream which we can see running away with trees or bushes beside it transects the railway bridge. If you'd just point that out for us, please, Mr. Nort, where I indicated, with your finger. There it is. That's the bridge. Now, the allegation that you will know is that large numbers of villagers, escaping from the attack on their village, went along that streambed. First there was an attack on a large -- on a number of family members where people were killed. Second, there was an incident where women and men were separated from each other, the men were made to strip, were robbed of their property, and then were shot in large numbers. Were you present in the area of Bela Crkva at the time early on the morning that it is said this happened or not? It's March the 25th, early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present early in the morning in the area of Bela Crkva, but everything that you've just said never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you say that, do you see? That's what I want you to help us with and that's why I gave you an opportunity to look at the map earlier -- not the map, the visual aid earlier, and tell us, how do you say that none of this happened, please? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply because my unit was there in the area, and I know that I passed through Bela Crkva and that there was no action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that there is quite a lot of illogical things that you state. In the indictment, at least where I saw it, they said they fled along the stream of Belaja, which means that they could not have fled to the south and towards the bridge that you just mentioned, but if they're going along the stream, then they're moving north towards Milanovac mountain, and that's why I can say that that did not happen, because they would be moving upstream.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd just have a look at some of the next photographs that I'd like you to have a look at, please. You see -- I'll hand you a photograph. This boy, aged 14, is one of those whose body was found. Put it on the overhead projector. Can you explain for us, please, from contemporaneous records or accounts given to you by your colleagues how a 14-year-old boy got shot in Bela Crkva on the morning when you were so near that you tell us you know exactly what happened. How did he get shot?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I be of assistance to you when my assertions basically and fundamentally differ from your question and what you're saying. My experience is quite different, so how do you expect me to know that, and I claim that that never happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, from the family group that it is said by eyewitnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has a point. Let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will be some misunderstanding later on because in the transcript it says the witness has been speaking of them moving towards Milanovac mountain, and here it says "land mountain." The name of the mountain isn't recorded in the transcript. It says "Milan vac mountain" but he said "Milanovac mountain." That's the name of the mountain; Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at these photographs, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the point that's just been made, I didn't understand the answer. Mr. Vukovic, you gave some answer about the movement of the villagers being illogical. You say that it was claimed in the indictment they fled along the stream of Belaja, which means they could not have fled to the south and towards the bridge. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bonomy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because the Belaja stream flows from the village of Bela Crkva in the direction of north-south, and south of the village of Bela Crkva, running one kilometre or one and a half kilometres, where it flows into the river called Beli Drim. So if they were fleeing from the village along the stream, they were not able to go to the south. If they were going upstream they couldn't have gone to the south towards the railway bridge but to the north towards Milanovac mountain, which is north of Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That depends on the expression "upstream," is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it you accept that the railway bridge is a bridge over the Belaja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume there's an old bridge there. I didn't cross the bridge, but across that stream there must be a bridge because there's a railway line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed, Mr. Vukovic, there's one railway bridge -- one railway line. There's the one stream that runs from Bela Crkva, and the evidence before this Court and the material provided to independent gatherers of information about Bela Crkva comes from eyewitnesses who are describing their own village. Do you not accept that people describing their own Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. village will know that the stream is crossed by a bridge at a unique place when they describe it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't comment on their statements. I said that if you went along the stream you wouldn't come that way. You wouldn't come across a bridge. I know what I said very well. Possibly there's also an error in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have a look at -- and it's necessary, because this is what this case is about. And I'm going to suggest to you this is one of the reasons that you're so anxious to hide from Bela Crkva. You see these pictures? First, a girl. It's a girl aged 9. Next picture, please. Two children. I'm afraid I can't identify which of the two of the three. One 6 and one 7. Their bodies, shot dead, were found, and the evidence is that they were killed on this day. You were in the area. Can you give us any explanation for how or why they died?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not hiding anything. I think that's what you said. Secondly, I cannot give you any proof or evidence of how they died because I keep telling you that there was no action on that day in the village of Bela Crkva. And as far as I know, and I do know for certain, right up until the 28th of March there was no action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're lying, Mr. Vukovic, and I'm going to prove you're lying to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have those documents back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have told --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I would like to ask you something, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a right which you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us that the orders that you should attack Bela Crkva came to nothing because you received intelligence that there was no KLA there. Can you now please point us to any contemporaneous report that shows that you received any such intelligence?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that an order meant nothing to me, the order that you quoted meant nothing to me. But had you read the rules of service carefully, you would be able to see the procedure and conduct of each and every soldier, including the commanding officer, what they're supposed to do when in a concrete situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe there's a translation difficulty. It wasn't said in English to you that the order meant nothing to you. The point that was made was that the order, the attack -- the order that you should attack Bela Crkva came to nothing - in other words, was not implemented - because you received intelligence that there was no KLA there. So you were not insulted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, would you now please answer --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, that's quite a different matter, then, and I can explain why the village of Bela Crkva was not searched, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's much more specific than that. The question is what contemporaneous document is there you can point to that says there was an intelligence report to the effect that there were no KLA there? So where is the documents that confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, in a -- in battle, in every combat operation, you don't keep notes. My courier cannot carry a laptop with him and write out orders during a combat operation. You command in combat directly and through your communication devices, and my subordinate informed me that he had passed through Bela Crkva, that he had taken up positions east of the village of Bela Crkva, and that he had come into contact with the police unit there, he had established contact, and that there was no action in the village. So those are relevant facts on the basis of which I made my decision to pass through the village of Bela Crkva in a column for only one reason; not to tire my men and have to walk through. So that was the only reason. And my commander that very morning had passed through Bela Crkva himself, and he personally saw what I had done and the measures I had taken. So there is no space or time there to write out documents. You don't write documents. There are no such documents. No army in the world writes out documents in combat situations. Before an action takes place -- this is done before and after an action take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]..."As Seen, As Told." Apart from witnesses who have come and given evidence here themselves directly, I'd like you to consider, please, extract from the book "As Seen, As Told." We have it for you in B/C/S, or Serbian, if you prefer. And if Mr. Nort could place -- point that to the witness and place that on the overhead projector. I'm grateful. Now, you tell us that you looked at extracts from this book preparatory to providing your statements, and if we look at what was reported by "As Seen, As Told" about Bela Crkva, we can see, and I shan't go through all of it, but if you follow the paragraphs as I read them out. The first paragraph deals with the location. The second paragraph says: "Only a few hours after the search of -- after the start of bombing ... Serb forces occupied the village. Much of the population --"

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you're reading from. I can't follow. And generally speaking, I don't know what you've given me. I have the book that I had in my hands, and I have no idea what it is that you have. It's some typewritten text that means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have the "As Seen, As Told" Serbian edition with you in your hands. Would you be good enough to make it available to me just for a minute. We've been hoping to find a copy --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Just please do not mix up the pages that I've marked. I need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at that, please. You're now reading from a passage that starts off with: "Bela Crkva lies 7 miles south-east ..." Next paragraph: "Only a few hours after the start of NATO bombing Serb forces occupied the village." Then it says, next sentence: "In the early hours of the 25 of March, VJ and police arrived ... with tanks, positioned them on a hill, began shelling ... the homes and burning the village. Villagers fled in different directions, but many failed to escape. Rounded up money, extorted in exchange for lives." Next paragraph: One group fled to a valley half a kilometre away where police and VJ surrounded them. Women and children allowed to leave, men placed in a yard, money demanded. Next paragraph: Another group of 2 to 300 were trying to escape the shelling of Bela Crkva --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot follow. You read much too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll read more slowly. We're now on the fourth paragraph. "Meanwhile, another group of 200-300 villagers who were trying to escape the shelling of Bela Crkva fled towards the Beli Drim river which flows southwards from Bela Crkva towards Rogovo. The UCK arrived and advised the people to move on as paramilitaries were advancing. The police were all around. One group made their way along the stream and hid under the railway bridge." Now, just pause there. This is a very detailed account. You'll see it's got what are called footnotes which identify the number of witnesses who provided -- or sources of material who provided information to those who prepared this particular document. The footnotes from this go from number 32 to 44 and are a very large number of different sources. Are you saying, please, from your knowledge that each and every word of this is false, made up?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with your leave let's take it one by one. It says: "Just a few hours later ..." That's not true. The bombing started exactly at 19.59. My unit was in the area of the village around 5.30, so around 11 hours later. Let's go on. It says, "Serb forces occupied the village." They probably mean both the army and police. What kind of Serb forces I had I already proved to you by describing the ethnic structure of my unit. Furthermore, Serb forces cannot occupy a village which is located on the sovereign territory of that country. That's a lie. Since you are using at that expression, I will be using it too. It says, "Entered Bela Crkva --" first entered and then shelled. Who would be mad enough, Mr. Nice, to get in their own forces? And no matter which page of this book you turn I'll prove to you on the basis of facts that it's a lie. Then references to arson and torching. Bring back that picture and you will see how narrow the streets are in Bela Crkva. If only one house had been set on fire there, my tank and soldiers would have burnt as well. It says: "The people were later released and directed to Zrze village." Zrze village is to the south-west the Bela Crkva. And then it says they fled to the mountains. Give me that image that you showed a moment ago, that visual aid, and show me where that mountain is they fled into. Then it goes on to say they fled into the mountains and then we found them, we robbed them a little, raped them a little, burned them a little, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and so on and so forth. I can contest each and every one of these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... of some of these details. If we'd just look at the one little paragraph, on the right-hand side of the page, Mr. Nort. A little bit further up. That's it there, the one on the right there now. "Fifty-five men were separated from the women and children. The women and children were ordered to leave. The 55 men were forced to strip to the waist and stand with their hands behind their head while they were searched. A bullet was found in the pocket of a 13-year-old boy." That's the boy we've already looked at in the photographs. "Police were told the boy had picked it up on the road. The men were asked if anybody supported the boy's statement and the boy's uncle stepped forward. He was taken to one side -" and he was the local doctor, I think - " ... and a burst of gunfire was heard and the uncle fell." Now, there's a direct description of events. Do you say this is all being made up or, and I want you to think about this before you answer, may it be that the police or reservists or even people being or resembling paramilitaries did this and you didn't see it or don't choose to remember that you heard about it. May these things have been done by other people?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm giving you a chance, Mr. Vukovic. You see, you're the army. Let me just explain: So far as this part of Kosovo is concerned, the army gets a number of adverse mentions from witnesses and other sources but often it's the police who are identified, or reservists who are identified, or Serbs, local Serbs who are identified as the killers. Now, just think back. Take your time. Is it possible that these things actually happened and you didn't see them, or are you saying for sure that they didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this question you put forward a lot of propositions. You mentioned some armed civilians and paramilitaries, if I understood you correctly. There was certainly no paramilitaries. There were no paramilitaries. I can guarantee that, because I know my commander well and I know myself, and I know the orders that I had received. First of all, when we're talking about this anti-terrorist action, I don't need time to think. I know what I know, and I am telling you that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you are asking me whether I allow the possibility that it was done by somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The answer is coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that those things did not actually happen or that they might have happened and you didn't see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry to be putting it this way, but you're asking me a very ambiguous question. I am telling you that the army certainly did no such thing. And who else could have done it, if you look at these maps, apart from my soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask: How long in the course of the day were you in Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day, I spent about 30 minutes in Bela Crkva. When I say "I spent," I mean my entire unit. That's the time we needed to pass through the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And while you were there, did you see any of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already told you that the MUP unit also passed through the village of Bela Crkva on the way to their line of blockade to the village of Velika Krusa. All this, including this bridge, was behind the blockade line. There was simply no forces there, either of the army or the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long was your unit in the company of a MUP unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout this anti-terrorist action, we were together because the action is named "Provision of support to MUP units."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this occasion and probably only on this occasion I'm going to ask you to look at another source. Again not our witnesses. They may have been the same witnesses, they may not, but differently collected by Human Rights Watch in their book "Under Orders." It's the same passage, it's on page 348 of this document which is Exhibit 145, and I'm afraid it doesn't come in B/C/S but I'll just read the passage to you in English, and it will be interpreted for you. This deals with the passage on the bridge, and it's something that we have indeed had in evidence ourselves here. A bit further up, please. A tiny bit further. And it reads as follows: "According to the witnesses, an Albanian doctor from Bela Crkva named Nesim Popaj, aged thirty-six, tried to negotiate with the Serbian commander, pleading with him to spare the lives of the villagers. Popaj allegedly explained that they were not members of the KLA but just villagers who wanted to work in peace. The commander responded by saying: 'You're terrorists, bring out your guns.'"
