"During this discussion, witnesses said the commander was stepping down on the neck of Shendet Popaj, the doctor's seventeen-year-old nephew, who was lying prone on the ground. Abruptly ending the discussion, the commander - described by one witness as a medium-height man, around thirty-five ... in a green camouflage uniform with three stars on his shoulder - shot Dr. Popaj with three bullets in front of his wife and three children, after which he killed Shendet." And then this: "The witness noted specifically that the commander, believed by the witness to be a captain, had a distinguishing feature: A recognisably deformed mouth." And there are other witness statements, I must tell you, Mr. Vukovic, which deal with the -- or there are witness statements that deal with this captain's unusual mouth. Two things: As to Human Rights Watch Report, have you read it yourself or had parts of it read or interpreted to you before?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have not read that. I had -- the first volume was quite sufficient to me to understand what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second, do you say that the account given here is necessarily and on the basis of your personal experience wholly untrue?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to comment at all nor am I in a position to comment on the statements of people whom I don't know. I suppose that this book, too, was created in June 1999 and that statements were taken from Siptars who had crossed over to Albania or to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must tell me when the book was written. Otherwise, the names of these people mean nothing to me and their statements either. I don't know whether they existed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not under obligation to do anything, but I'll tell you that its publication of this version is 2001. Its methodology has been gone into extensively before this Court, and I now come to my last question: Does a captain in a green camouflage uniform with a distinguishingly unusual mouth bring anyone to your mind? Does it remind you of anyone?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in the unit or in the army, there were no deformed people. And second, it is well known that usual procedure is to send into disability retirement anyone who is not fit for military service. I myself have a disability pension. There were no deformed people, so how could I think of anyone? Second -- third, a captain cannot be a commander. It's a lower-ranking officer. He can command a platoon or a company at best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does a captain have three stars on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A captain has three stars on his shoulder. So does a colonel, except that the colonel has, in addition, a gold line here and laurel leaves embroidered and things like that. So that's also a distinguishing characteristic of a colonel's uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the statement you made for the commission about this topic. It's originally Delic tab 362. Now, as I understand it, the reason you didn't search the -- or that there was no search of Bela Crkva was that you had intelligence that there was no terrorist activity there; is that right? All quiet.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that came from whom?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you: From the commander of my forward security detail. Generally speaking, when a unit is marching, it has forward security at the head that secures the march until the point of destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, this is the document made on the 10th of January, 2003, and then at the bottom of the page on display we see this for the -- well, better pick it up in the middle. You set out the assignment of Combat Group 2 was to search the village of Bela Crkva, break through to trig 432, to destroy the STS in Celine-Nogavac. And then in the last paragraph, it says: "On the 25th of March ... carried out the march ... took up positions along the lines of the blockade by 0630. The task of forward security was to establish whether STS were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. present along the march route to search the village of Bela Crkva. And then together with 4/27 special police detachment and enable Combat Group 2 to take up positions --"

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you're reading from, I'm sorry. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fifth paragraph of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case read the entire paragraph, because what you're reading makes no sense. It is in no way linked with the paragraph I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... paragraph beginning on the 25th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's the fifth paragraph in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About six lines down, it says this: "Upon leaving the village of Zrze we waited by the silo for our unit from Prizren to pass and that is where the forward support commander contacted me and informed me he had not --" over the page, please, Mr. Nort -- "searched the village of Bela Crkva because parts of the 23rd Special Police Unit detachment were already in the village." So what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have read it, but it's obviously not a good translation. But -- because in my version, it says, "He informed me that he had not performed a search of Bela Crkva village," whereas the interpretation I'm getting is that he had performed a search.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whether I didn't read the word not out, I'm not sure

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I did. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He hadn't searched the village because parts of the 23rd Special Police Unit detachment were already in the village. So what were they doing, the 23rd Special Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a company of that detachment, and they were doing exactly the same thing as I: They were on their way to take up positions on the blockade line from which they were to start executing the assignment, and they were passing through the village. Because in the village itself there was a bridge across this Belaja stream, and they had to go over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I asked you was -- just have a look. What were they doing? You give us an account. The next question is this: How do you know what they were doing? Did they report to you? Did you hear it over the radio? Did you have a meeting afterwards? Did they send you a written report? What?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not report to each other, either the army to the police or the police to the army. I'm telling you what I saw. It's a little hard to explain to you military activities because you're not a soldier. For instance, I come to an intersection in the village. I stop my vehicle. I stand on the intersection, and I direct various parts of my units, showing them where to go, because I know the map a little better, I know topography a little better. I went into commander's reconnaissance before this assignment, and I saw that the police were going along their axis. And generally speaking, I would have heard if there had been any activities. It was 5.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, when you were passing through the village, were you with the whole of the 23rd Special Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In this action, it was not the whole unit that took part, only the 4th Company of that police detachment. They were not complete and my unit was not complete either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But were the whole group that were intended to participate in the blockade with you, were they all with you when you went through Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could not have been all with me because there were certainly 150, 200 people there. I have in the analysis document the exact number of people in that company. And I'm telling you again even my whole unit was not there at the moment because one part of the unit had continued on the way to Brinje village and then turned east to assume their axis of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my question then is the reference to the activity of your officer who advised you about the circumstances in Bela Crkva simply says part of the 23rd Special Police Unit detachment were already in the village, and that's ahead of you. So how is it that you know what they were doing from your own personal knowledge, which is what you founded your answer on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it says here "because parts of the 23rd Special Police detachment were already in the village." And I'm basing my statement precisely on what I -- what I heard and what I saw, because it is from 5.00, 5.30 until 6.00 max. It is still dark, and you can hear extremely well any kind of activity. You can see any kind of activity, the sort of activity Mr. Nice refers to, like the burning of houses. I'm telling you those things didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, your answer is not satisfactory at all. Do you know at all what they were doing at the time? And if you knew anything, how -- how do you know what they were doing? All I have heard from you is that have there been anything you have heard something from the -- but which is not satisfactory to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I could know about their activities is what I saw myself or heard myself or what was reported to me by one of my platoon commanders in that area, if anything. Otherwise, we didn't submit reports to each other, the army to the police or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, you have been specific. You've said that the only thing they did was pass through on their way to take up positions on the blockade line, and what we want to know is what was the advance group, the group that was there before you were there, what were they doing. And it seems very difficult at the moment to understand how you would know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On that note, I think we have to take the break. Do you want to answer that? If you wish to answer that, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly I would like to answer. I don't want to stop here. How a commander knows what his unit is doing: He knows on the basis of the report filed. I had radio communication during the march. We call it, by the way, radio silence. The radio equipment is on, and we hear from each other only if there is a specific need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me read one of your answers. On this very point, Mr. Nice asked you, "What were they doing? You give us an account." The next question is this: "How did you know what they were doing? Did they report to you? Did you hear it over the radio? Did you have a meeting afterwards? Did they send you a report? What?" And your answer: "We did not report to each other, either the army to the police or the police to the army. I'm telling you what I saw. It's a little hard to explain to you military activities because you're not a soldier," and then you go away on a frolic of your own about military activities being things that we and the Prosecutor can't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, you confused my answers. This answer that you're reading now was in response to whether I knew what the police units were doing, and a few moments ago we were talking about what my own organ did, those who were providing security for me during the march, part of my own unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just listen to the part that leads up to the answer I've just quoted to you. The question was, and this is about your advanced officer who reported back to you: "He hadn't searched the village because parts of the 23rd Police Special detachment were already in the village. So what were they doing, the 23rd Police Special Unit?" And your answer: "This is a company of that detachment, and they were doing exactly the same thing as I: They were on their way to take up positions ..." You were answering exactly the same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's right, but I don't see what it is that troubles you here. I received reports from my subordinate officers. I quite simply don't understand what kind of answer you want from me. I get reports only from my own junior officers, or soldiers, if it's easier for you to follow that way what I'm saying. And he reported to me that there had been no activity in the village, that policemen were in the village, that they were moving towards the blockade line. I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe what Judge Bonomy is saying is that that, what you have just said, contradicts what you said earlier that there were no reports, that you received no reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm saying that there were no reports between the police and the army, whereas this officer of mine is a soldier just like I am, and he comes from my very own unit. And it is only natural that he should report to me orally when we see each other as to what he did, what he had done. So this is reporting the combat security going through Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand it, your previous answer, you're saying, was that there were no reports between the police and the army. Your present answer relates to reports inter se, reports between your own soldiers and yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Between the leader of that head security and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have gone past the one-hour break, so we'll take the 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we just have a look at the last part of your statement to the VJ commission on this, please. It's still on the overhead projector, I think. Yes. You ended your account of this event to the VJ commission by saying that you first heard in late 2001 about the crimes allegedly committed in the Bela Crkva sector, but where did you learn about it in late 2001?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date, but the indictment was issued against Mr. Milosevic. It was in the newspapers, on television. It was discussed rather extensively. I heard from my colleagues, too, who had also heard about it in one of those ways, and we talked about that quite a bit, at least with the people who were accessible to me at the time. I don't know exactly when the indictment was issued against Mr. Milosevic, but I think it was already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it came from the Milosevic indictment. Incidentally, was the work of the --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you didn't hear about it from the Milosevic indictment, where did you hear about these allegations from?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you. I'm telling you where I heard about it from. I never read the indictment as a whole, but parts of those -- of that indictment were carried by the newspapers, television. So in that way I and my colleagues learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally, it's right, isn't it, that the VJ commission, or the Commission for Cooperation - we'll come to the title in detail later - was trying to respond to allegations in the Milosevic indictment. That was the focus of its work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you're saying. That's not what I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then, if not, what was the focus of its work? Because this was a commission with very senior people, with people who have been indicted before this Tribunal now for complicity in events like Srebrenica at a very high level. What was the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're putting a question that I can certainly not give an answer to. It's as if you asked me what's the basic task of your office, the Office of the Prosecutor, is. Also, I cannot give an answer to that because I have no idea what you do. So I cannot tell you about such things. Also about this commission, I absolutely do not know what they dealt with because I didn't take part in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your statement concludes -- if you can't help further, I'll move to your statement. Your statement says: "I read something about them in the book 'As Seen, As Told' published by the Humanitarian Law Centre. Since I am disgusted by the author and the fabrications she sets out in the book, I didn't finish reading it." Is that really your position as a serious soldier, that you didn't finish reading the allegations about the place where you were said to be an officer in charge?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have completely misinterpreted what I wrote. I read it, and I even made photocopies from this book of excerpts that have to do with my unit and areas where my unit was. But I didn't read it to the end, because when I see all the lies that are put forth in cases where I was personally, then why would I read about Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't see why I would read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just for the cite, please, the original book that you've got there. If Mr. Nort would bring it to us. We just want to have a look at how it appears in that version. We've been seeking such a copy. But -- thank you very much. Were you under the impression that Natasa Kandic was the author of this book?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the front page and the back page, it says the Fund for Humanitarian Law, translated by them, I guess, and then -- for the publisher Natasa Kandic. I think that is what is written there, but then if you give me the book, I'll show you where it is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you wrote this passage in your statement, did you actually read anything about the methodology of this book, the way in which its sources had been identified and the way in which the research had been carried out? Did you?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's written in the foreword, and on that basis I came to the conclusion I came to as to what the value of this book could be. I saw whose statements were taken from and where these statements were taken. It couldn't have been any better than what it actually is. If you want to us talk about the Fund for Humanitarian Law, I can discuss that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think we have time for that at the moment. Now, nothing of any kind happened in Bela Crkva on the 25th, 26th of March, 1999, yes?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wrote in my statement, too, and I say -- I claim that my unit did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any subsequent fighting in Bela Crkva; and if so, on what days?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain, because the last time I went round the outskirts of Bela Crkva was on the 2nd of April when I was returning from completing my combat task. Until then, I can guarantee that I saw absolutely no effects in terms of destruction, et cetera. Now, later on, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Vukovic. Look at this, please.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not lying. You are lying, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not lying. You are lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are you going to leave from this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to leave the statement, yes, but I'm quite happy to stay with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put it on the ELMO again, please. Mr. Vukovic, the last sentence of this statement I think is a bit different from the answer you just gave to us now. Here you said, "I also do not know anything about whether another unit committed the alleged crime." This is different from what you stated earlier today. You said had there been anything, you would have known that, which means that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon. Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt. Let me finish my answer -- question, and after having heard the answer, I'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm saying. That's what I said today too. In the statement it says so as well. "I also do not know anything about whether another unit committed the alleged crime." That's what I've been saying all along. I absolutely have no knowledge of any other unit having done it, my unit or a police unit. For my own unit, I claim that because they were with me all the time and they could not have been elsewhere at that point in time. So I don't think it differs from what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not exclude the possibility of this crime having happened that -- by another unit or by those who you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, that would be as if you asked me about the region of Pristina, Subotica, Cacak. How can I talk about things that I did not see and places that I did not go to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, we are dealing with the alleged crime which happened in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's right. And I'm saying to you that while I was in the village of Bela Crkva, there was no action because I would have had to see it and I would have had to hear it. Since I did not hear it or see it, that means that it didn't happen. I cannot talk hypothetically about whether in three days or five days or in a month somebody committed a crime. War in itself is a crime, and if it was committed, it certainly was not committed on anybody's orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Confine your answer. Be very simple. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, this last sentence as you quoted it is incorrectly translated. Incorrectly translated when Colonel Vukovic read it, too, because there is no question mark. It also says: "I do not know that another unit committed an alleged crime." It doesn't say about "whether." It says: "I also do not know that another unit committed the alleged crime." There is no "whether."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that there is a difference, but thanks for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, what colour uniform were you wearing on this day?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colour of the uniform of all members of my unit was camouflage. It was a camouflage uniform, and the basic colour was green. There's also brown, and there's also lighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at these photographs, please. These photographs taken in June of 1999 show, do they not, destruction on an enormous scale of this village. Look at the one you're looking at now. Houses with their roofs off. The next one, please, Mr. Nort. More of the same. Houses destroyed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Next one, please. Can you explain for us, as the person who had local knowledge and local -- a local role to play, can you explain, please, how those buildings got damaged in that way? This is Exhibit 167 -- 157, tab 2, part of. Can you explain, please, how these got damaged in this way?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain or comment on these pictures that you're showing me now. I can testify to you only about the period in which my unit was in that area. That's what I keep telling you all the time, and you keep asking me different things. How can I explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I explain a destroyed house? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You and maybe the police, but since you don't wish to assert it was somebody else, maybe it was you on your own, I don't know, you were engaged in cleansing this area, weren't you? It's quite simple.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not my men, certainly, but I and my men took part in this anti-terrorist action, but Bela Crkva was not involved at all. There was no action by my unit in Bela Crkva. And as far as I know, of no other unit either in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, could you just put the other two quick pictures on in succession in case one of them shows what I want it to show. Next one, please. No. In which case, can you just take this one instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help us, please, from your local knowledge: The village in the distance -- the village in the distance there - it's not very far away - what village is that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be the village of Rogovo. Yes, it is the village of Rogovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because it -- the bridge can be seen on the Beli Drim River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Before I move on to the next point in relation to Bela Crkva - if I can have the photographs back, please - so that we've now seen how near Rogovo is, a couple of points: Would you accept the following proposition that at the time with which we are dealing, March of 1999, KLA strongholds were to be found at the following villages or towns: Drenovac, Medari, Dragobilje, Malisevo, and Nisa. Would you accept those are the places where the KLA was at its strongest?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Pirane, Randubrava, and Donje Retimlje and Retimlje were other strongholds too. There was even the headquarters of a Siptar brigade in Retimlje. And Pagarusa is referred to and Dobrodeljane, et cetera. You have that in the order of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly none of the villages with which we are concerned, Bela Crkva, Celine, Velika Krusa, none of those place was a KLA stronghold?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course it was. I talked about it all of last week. The Podrinje-Pastrik operative zone was established. The mainstay was precisely this 124th Terrorist Brigade. But if you look at item 1 carefully and read it carefully - this is document number 3 among my documents - this is the order of the brigade commander, and you will see that -- I'm trying to find the exact section. Here it is. Local staffs. That is in the first paragraph, the second bullet. So the 124th Brigade of the KLA, about 300 terrorists. Retimlje is its command post. The command post of the operative zone Podrinje Pastrik and of the KLA is in the village of Malaria. That is to the north of this place but on Milanovac mountain. Also it says local staffs, and in brackets, 500 [as interpreted] to 100 terrorists in Gornja/Donja Potocari, the village of Nespelje [phoen], Velika Krusa, Basik ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- armed settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 50 to 100 terrorists is a slip of the tongue, I think. The only named place is Velika Krusa and then only as 50 to 100 terrorists. The strongholds, I suggest, were the places to the north that I've identified; Drenovac, Medari, Dragobilje, Malisevo, and Nisa.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The major strongholds were always in the area of Drenica and the area of Mount Milanovac. But read the entire paragraph and you will see that there are these local guards, consisting of 50 to 100 terrorists, in all villages at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Totally unconnected question: The 72nd Special Police Unit -- sorry, Special VJ Unit, tell us about that. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean what do I know about that? Are you interested in that period or where they are now or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 72nd Special VJ Unit was what, commanded from Belgrade? Was crack troops, expensively trained and armed, and only to be used for special operations. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 72nd Special Brigade, that is its name, such a unit did exist. If you're asking me whether part of that unit was in Kosovo and Metohija, I know it was. A small part of it was there, perhaps one or two companies, I cannot tell you exactly, because I encountered them in 1998. A few times we even participated together in some anti-terrorist actions. But I cannot give you any more specific information about this unit; I never worked in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They were only used for very special events, weren't they, because they were such a prized and valued unit.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fighting against terrorists is a special task. All countries use special units first and foremost in combatting terrorism, as we currently witness elsewhere in the world. It is quite natural that this unit should be used for anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were they doing in Rogovo?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just as if you were asking me about an SAS unit, what it was doing in Iraq. How could I know what they were doing in Rogovo? And you didn't tell me the date or the time or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 25th of March, 1999, what they were doing in Rogovo? 25th, 26th, 27th, 30th, what were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all. I have no information that in that period that unit was in Rogovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Rogovo would be easily connected via that streambed to the railway bridge, wouldn't it? Just go along the streambed beyond the railway bridge and you land up on the road to Rogovo. We saw it on the map.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take that stream you'll get exactly to the river of Beli Drim. Not to Rogovo but to Beli Drim. And the Belaja stream or brook flows into the Beli Drim. I can show you that on the map where it can be seen very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I want to check before I move to my next topic that you stand by, as I think you have in various answers to me and also to the Court, answers that you gave yesterday about Bela Crkva. At 10.29 -- not necessarily yesterday; on day 431. You said: "The search of Bela Crkva was not carried out, because I said that my lead security, my forward security, whose assignment is to ensure unhindered march for my combat group on their axis of movement, established through reconnaissance that there was no activity from Bela Crkva village against our troops. Since there was no activity against us, there was no reason for us to counteract." Do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I stand by that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the same day at 11.00, no minutes and six seconds, you said: "Bela Crkva village is completely outside the area of conduct of military operations. So this is absolutely incorrect. We never surrounded Bela Crkva village, and we never performed any operations in it because there was no attack." Do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, may we turn, please, to your diary, which needs again interpretation and reading problems. Can we place -- just at the moment can we just place a full version of the diary on the overhead projector so that we can understand its format.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nort, if you'd be good enough simply to display the first page when you get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the very first page of this diary, we see it starts off with entries for the 24th of March, but I think - help me if I'm wrong - not in your hand.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This handwriting is the handwriting of one of my assistants. I judge that by his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We do have some translations for this part of the diary. If they could now be distributed. I'll go through the first half dozen pages so that we can understand what was written. By the way, remember yesterday -- while this is being distributed, remember yesterday, Mr. Vukovic, I asked you in simple, short sentences to describe what it was you were doing in the operations at Bela Crkva and elsewhere? Do you remember my asking you those questions?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I did answer some questions put to me, such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just let me find my notes. Yesterday, in describing in your own terms what happened at this time and in this area, you spoke of an anti-terrorist operation. You used the word "blockade," "search," and then there was a discussion about the word "destruction," and about the use of the word "destruction" or "uncover." You used the word "blocking off," "breaking up the enemy," and you also used the word "neutralise." Do you remember using all those words yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are my terms. Well, not my terms but military terms and, yes, did I use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 24th of March of 1999, your colleague or subordinate set out an entry: "NATO forces committed aggression on the territory of FRY, against military targets in Belgrade..." and so on. I'm not going to read all of these, we don't have time. 2120: All systems in full readiness ... 2300: Declaration of state of war. 0200: BG2 went to perform the task 1278 from the 23rd of March order, 186 people engaged. 0230: From the direction of the Republic of Albania intensive reconnaissance of the NATO Air Force. And then we turn to the next day, the 25th of March. So that's the entries for the 24th of March. 25th of March: "Commander 3A and Commander PRK praised all units for extremely brave attitude and professionalism in performing their tasks in the beginning of NATO armed aggression." And then it says this: "On LP Zub arrived something brigade of anti-aircraft defence," and then some more --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-propelled battery PVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 26th of March: "Urgent measures undertaken for illegible taking out of materiel and equipment from the dump in the barracks in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For fortification and pulling out materiel and technical resources from the warehouse in the Djakovica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then on the same day at 2005, a reference to the dump with ammunition being hit. On the 27th, a reference to a part of the road, commander of an engineering platoon, and other entries. There's one, for example, at 2100, action with the --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mining a certain direction towards Albania. Axis towards Albania. Concretely our territory at the Cafa Prusit border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come to 2100, action with a Praga anti-aircraft gun. 1800 to 2100, strength of one detachment destroyed in the region. Doesn't make -- can't be read. Assignment successfully completed by the unit which is in charge. What does that mean, by the way, the 1800 to 2100 passage?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says or, rather, a terrorist group appeared there numbering about 12 men in the Prisak [phoen] area of the -- Prisak village, which is away from the village of Zub, to the east of my command post, actually, some ten kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We then go on to the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, if you've got that on the overhead projector, bottom of the left-hand page. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 28th of March, Zub and wider area directly attacked by rockets, two of which were aimed for systems. After rockets appeared, and so on, in reference to Djakovica and so on. So that takes us until the 28th of March --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in the evening. Then the handwriting changes. Is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's still the handwriting of probably some soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably some soldier?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you take a look, you'll find the same handwriting in some of the previous documents, reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And an officer or, rather, if a soldier makes the entries, the officer dictates the entry to be made. And my handwriting is to be found from the third -- let me see. Let me just check that. No, that's not my handwriting either, none of it here either. For the 2nd, I see that I did make some entries personally. Part of the entries were made by me personally because I state that the unit was just completed on the 3rd again because it was an in different positions along different axes previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... let's go back to where we were on the document. It says, "Amendment of the war record," doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's what it says on page 4, "Amendment to the war record."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you authorise that amendment? Pretty important document, a war diary. Did you authorise that amendment?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorisation for that amendment could have been issued either by me or by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have no reason to doubt what follows, do we? What follows is an official record and the only contemporaneous record we have of anything that happened in this area between the 25th and the 30th of March. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this is the only document in which mention is made of the activities of the unit for that particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Then let's explain how the 25th of March has been amended. 0130, that's the time you set off. March was done in the direction Zub-Djakovica-Zrze-Bela Crkva in order to accomplish assignment. In the course of marching, and then there's something that hasn't been deciphered, vehicles TAM 130, T10 number plates, two soldiers injured, Dragan Milanovic and Boban Velkovic [phoen]. And then this: Villages Bela Crkva were blocked and cleaned, or cleansed. There were no losses.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you explain to us, please, how at a date no earlier than the 28th of March, and notwithstanding everything you've told us about Bela Crkva being left untouched, your war diary reflects the fact that it was cleansed?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an addition, Mr. Nice, and you can see that it was written, at the earliest, on the 28th of March, because what follows after that -- it follows on after that date. I was not at my command post on the 28th either, and most probably a device was used to inform my deputy where the unit was for a very short space of time, because you can't use the device for any length of time because you're located by the enemy and targeted. So it's just a brief piece of information, saying where the unit was and what part of the assignment had been carried out. On the 25th, the closer assignment was carried out and automatically, pursuant to the brigade commander's instructions, he recorded the previous points. And if you look, you will see that it coincides exactly with what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand you. This entry makes it clear that far from being free of attack, Bela Crkva was cleansed, and I'd like you, please, to tell the Judges how come your war diary contains that entry.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just answered that. Well, I can't even remember, but with my deputy, I heard him over the radio communication device regularly, and in the evening of the 25th I know that I informed him that in the unit there were no losses for the first day, that we were at that such-and-such line, and that we had carried out our task, our assignment. I didn't go on mentioning any villages because the message would have been too long; the radio station and communication line would have been detected and targeted. And then following an automatic process, he recorded this. Now, I've already explained to you why there was nothing in Bela Crkva. I explained that to you today and yesterday and the day before. I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At most on your account, which I don't for one second accept, if there had been misunderstanding, you would have been saying we searched Bela Crkva and there was nothing there. Your scribe has recorded a word "cleansed" or "cleaned," and that's because that's exactly what you were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is precisely not what we were engaged in, and it was how I said. This -- I did not dictate this text. This text was dictated by my deputy at the command post, and I just informed the deputy where my location was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the word used for cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Ciscenje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Ciscenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we look at the entry for the 26th of March to see how your deputy, if this is your explanation, recorded events. But before we go on, did your deputy have problems with the use of language? Was he in some way illiterate? Was he hard of hearing? Tell us. Or was he a competent military officer?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I've already told you that in the Yugoslav army, either then or now, there were not people that were in -- with disabilities, and you were able to see that during the aggression as well. When I say "you," I mean your country, because it took part in the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 26th of March: "We are continuing cleaning -" or cleansing - "in cooperation with the MUP until 12.00. In the skilled manoeuvre group, we entered the village of Donja Retimlje," as it reads. "First group Donja Retimlje, second group --" we can't read the word -- "Velika Krusa MBN --" an abbreviation that we don't understand but you may help us -- "Velika Krusa, soldier Dalibor Misic was wounded in his right foot. Soldier was brought into the Prizren hospital and soldier Desimir Todorovic was put in the hospital. The whole day the soldiers endured the strain excellently. Albanians are leaving their weapons down, changing clothes, and they run away." Any reason to doubt any part of that entry, including in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular the opening phrase, "We are continuing cleaning -" or cleansing "- in cooperation with the MUP"?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say in cooperation with or coordinate action. It says "coordinated action with MUP, weak, poor." Which means that we had certain problems along that line, precisely because the army was -- the military commander was in command of the army, the MUP unit was commanded by the MUP commander, and we did not have radio communication devices that were compatible. Now, as far as the continuation is concerned, on the 25th as well, if you want to -- me to use the word, we cleaned, or cleansed, the village of Celine, and Nogavac and Bela Crkva of terrorists. Of terrorists. So this refers to "ciscenje," the cleaning or cleansing exclusively as part of an operation against the terrorists, just as you use the word "cleaning" in everyday life where you're separating --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- something good from something bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's pause there for a minute, shall we? I asked you questions very carefully yesterday afternoon, not least so that it could be done before you had any chance to speak to anyone else, and I asked you what language you would use to describe what you did, and on no occasion did you use the word "cleansing." You used all sorts of other words. Now, are you now saying, and you said it, interestingly enough, in respect of Bela Crkva, that you were cleansing Celine, Nogavac, and Bela Crkva of terrorists? I thought there were no terrorists in Bela Crkva. What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once again you're distorting my words. I didn't say that these are my -- what I said. But when I use the word "ciscenje," cleaning, myself, anyway, this is what my deputy said and wrote, who was 20 kilometres away from me, at the battalion post. I didn't use these words. So it's just a question of terminology, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 25th, I state that he just copied it out automatically or, rather, copied out automatically what was said in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Just a minute. This is a -- you have to accept, Mr. Vukovic, this is a new explanation, therefore we must focus our attention on it. This, the only contemporaneous record of events, is simply not a contemporaneous record of things that actually happened because your deputy simply dictated something from an order without checking whether it actually happened. Is that what you're now suggesting?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is absolutely not what I'm saying. And that's not the only entry. You have an analysis of the brigade command, Mr. Nice. I have it under number -- just a moment, let me find what number -- number 5. And that is an authentic document, a contemporaneous document where or, rather, which clearly states according to the dates and times what was done in the area. And now you're saying that in my war diary something has been entered and recorded which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that that document, Delic's post facto analysis of events, describes Bela Crkva being cleansed? Have we missed something? Is it there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we read it together, we'll see whether it is there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is your explanation, Mr. Vukovic. Take the time to do it. Thank you. It's tab 359A. And you just take us to the passage where it's acknowledged that Bela Crkva was indeed cleansed.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably there is no mention of Bela Crkva because there was no action there, but, yes, I will skim through the document to see if I can find anywhere in it the village of Bela Crkva mentioned. It exists in the order because it was stated as an access -- axis, but it's not in the analysis because there was no action. But let me read out this entire document, or skim through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go to the second page and I think you'll find a reference to Bela Crkva on the -- right in the middle of the second page, and you'll find it on the second line.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I've made a note of that too. I highlighted that same paragraph. It is the first, second, third, fourth, fifth. It says this: "During the first day one of the close assignments was realised and a strong breakthrough was effected of the 23rd PJP from the direction of Bela Crkva and Brnjaca towards Celine and Mala Hoca." If we look at the map, you'll be able to see that axis, that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. Pause. It says nothing about cleansing Bela Crkva because your evidence has been consistent from first to last that nothing happened at Bela Crkva, and you've relied on these documents to support it. You're now suggesting that your deputy for some reason quoted from this document when he wrote the war diary. The entry you've just taken us to, or I've just taken you to to identify the word "Bela Crkva" doesn't support that. Do you want to find another entry that does?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not repeat this document anywhere. I repeated the order by the brigade commander for this anti-terrorist action, and in my files it is under number 3, and that is something that the deputy at the command post could have had. He could not have had an analysis at that time, which was compiled only on the 30th of March. So since -- how could he use an analysis compiled on the 30th on the 28th, for example? He couldn't. And, Mr. Nice, I did not receive this analysis myself. It is titled and addressed to the command of the Pristina Corps. That's who it's addressed to. And I said that my reports were incorporated in this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go now to the 27th of March. There are many more of these entries that we have to look at to get a complete picture of what you were up to. The 27th of March, all groups were merged until 0700. At 9.30 cleaning began in three directions. The first group, and then the direction is illegible, TT 356. The second group, and to us it's illegible but help us if you can for the 27th of March. The third group, Lieutenant Radojevic in the blockade --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One group took the direction of Retimlje and Neprebiste, and the other group took the direction of Retimlje-Mamusa, but I have to read it in order. The first group of Nedje Sela [phoen] from Donja Retimlje direction 350, trig 356. If we put the map up I'll be able to show you that point, the village of Neprebiste. The second group was by Lieutenant Jesi [phoen]. He was sent early in the morning pursuant to orders by the brigade commander. I sent him to quite a different -- in quite a different direction and axis to help Combat Group 1 which had been stopped in front of the village of Mahadzi because there was heavy firing coming from the terrorists. And the third group of Lieutenant Radojevic, his group, was in a blockade, which means he didn't move at all. About 600 hours -- 1600 hours a tank turned over, and when the operation was completed on the 27th, there was an order for the units to reconvene in the area of Mamusa, Neprebiste, Retimlje, Donja Retimlje, and for the units to return to their own area of deployment. In my unit, not in combat, a tank turned over, so I stayed there --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... evidence of that, writing about it, the tank turning over. Let's go to the next entry. 28th of March. I'll just read it out to you. Follow it, please: "Body of killed soldier Bojan Jovanovic was taken out, unit was transferred in groups to village - can't read the name of it - units were engaged in securing the state border according to the plan. In the course of the day around 2.000 people went in the direction of the border crossing Cafa." Cleansing had achieved its results, hadn't it? You were kicking out the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, well, I'm not -- I don't understand the interpretation I'm getting so I can't say whether you're commenting or asking me a question. Now, if you were asking me a question, then that is not true, it's not correct. And I can help you with something you asked me a moment ago from the 28th. This second paragraph is my writing, my handwriting in the war diary, because I had returned to my command post and to the end of the war I was a person -- I personally kept entries into this -- in this document. But as I say, what you just said a moment ago is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is your writing the writing in capital Cyrillic letters?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 28th, I used capital letters, Cyrillic capital letters, and from the 29th I used the Latin script, because I use both scripts in actual fact. I was taught both scripts at school so I use them intermittently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this is your handwriting from now on, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my handwriting, at least the portion that I have before me. Now, if you provide me with the whole war diary, I can leaf through it and give you a complete answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are going to take the 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Mr. Nort's assistance, we'll carry on with the diary entries so far as relevant. There are only a few more. We're on the 28th, which ends with 2.000 people going in the direction of the border crossing at Cafa. We then come to the 29th in Mr. Vukovic's hand. That reads as follow: "By order of the command of the 549th Motorised Brigade, confidential number 1304-1 --" Funnily enough, I can't -- yes, I can see that -- "platoon MB 120-millimetre was sent to Velika Hoca area - commander is Lieutenant Feta and he is subordinated to BG6 of the 519th Motorised Brigade. Remaining forces are ready for intervention in the direction Orahovac- village Ostrozub. The rest of the unit is undertaking assignments in depth security of the state border according to the plan." Then this: "In the course of the day around a thousand people went in the direction of the border crossing Cafa Prusit."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why are all these people on the move, please, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the reason why civilians were moving out, I spoke about that at length but I'll repeat what I said. The basic reason why the civilians were moving out or, rather, were leaving and going to Albania, Macedonia, Montenegro or other parts of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was fear from the bombing which started on the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that. Can we find any contemporaneous recording by you? Have you recorded that contemporaneously anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that any such thing can be found, especially not in the war diary, because what is entered into the war diary is only the most important activities of the unit, the most important events, not detailed reports. At any rate, I reported about these reasons. I reported to my brigade commander, and he compiled a piece of information that he sent on to the corps command. I have that piece of information here with me, and I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... if you're saying it's somehow important and significant. You mean it's in this diary? Because we're coming to the diary. We're going through the diary entries. We'll do them sequentially. Tell me, you saw the -- remember the pictures of Bela Crkva, of the houses with all the roofs off and burnt out, and there are -- we can see some more of Celine and probably of Velika Krusa and so on. What efforts were made to re-house the people who couldn't live in those houses?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean Bela Crkva specifically, the task of the army was not at all to put people up. This is done by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To protect. It's not the military units that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You drive by an area like Bela Crkva and you see that, good gracious me, all the houses have been burnt down, presumably you tell someone, and tell us what the civilian authorities did. Did they spring into action to suggest that these people go and live somewhere else, or did they bring them tents, or did they bring them prefabs, or did they kick them out and send them to Albania?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I did not say that I saw destroyed houses. That's what you're saying. I claim that while I was passing through Bela Crkva, I did not see anything unusual. Now, what the civilian organisations did is something that you have to ask them, because I was not on that terrain, and I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we return to the diary, do you remember you had an exchange with His Honour Judge Bonomy and His Honour Judge Bonomy pressed you as to whether you yourself had seen property being destroyed by your armaments, and eventually, after about two or three questions that you didn't answer, you acknowledged yes, you had seen property damaged and destroyed. Whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the question was related either to Celine or Randubrava. I cannot recall now. If you give me the transcript, I can talk about it. But I insisted that it was only places from which fire was opened at police units or military units, and in that case --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- anything is a legitimate --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour pressed you and tested your memory. You confirmed eventually that you'd seen property damaged and I'd like you to tell us which village. All right?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said. In the village of -- of Celine I saw that for sure because even my command post was shot at as it was being relocated. I also saw action in Randubrava, and I saw action in Donje Retimlje. I saw the effects of the action in Pirane. Because I was passing there, I saw the effects of the action in Velika Krusa and Mala Krusa in part. I saw the effects of the action in village of Medvjedce and partly in the village of Neprebiste because I got that far. I did not see anything in Mamusa because there was no action there, and in Bela Crkva I did not see anything because there had not been action. I cannot talk about Dobrodeljane, Noptarusa [phoen], and Suva Reka because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... also of damaged property. Forget the fact that it's not the army's responsibility, because the army has to work with the police. Tell us, from your knowledge, were any efforts made to deal with those whose property you'd seen destroyed and who were now without house? Any efforts made to help them? Apart from sending them to Albania or Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not sent to Albania and Macedonia. They went there on their own. Now, whether any efforts were made, to tell you the truth, I don't know because I was not involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in resolving problems like that. The task of my unit after this was to organise defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 29th of March, then. By order of the command of the 549th Motorised Brigade - this is of course still in your handwriting - confidential number 13041, platoon sent -- no, I've done this already. Sorry. 30th of March: "Following the order of the brigade command, around 0800 unit sent to blockade the village of -- to blockade of village Rogovo and in --" and perhaps you'd just like to check that I've got this right, in co-action or cooperation - I don't know what it is -- "with Brigade 3 and part of the 72nd Special Brigade, it --" let's just check on the word, as we can see it there. Oh, yes, is it "ciscenje" there, or "ciscenla" cleaned Rogovo?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "ocistila," and I'll tell you what it's about if you put a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all let's see if we can see what it actually says. So there you were with the 72nd Special Brigade, cleansing or cleaning the village of Rogovo, mahala Postra, mahala Ramahmat, and Mahadri mahala. And then it says there were no losses, and it goes on to say the following: "The rest of the unit is undertaking assignments in depth security of the state border according to the plan." I'll read the last bit, which in fact you touched on with the accused later, but let's just deal with the first number of lines. You tell us what you meant by cleaning the village of Rogovo, mahala Postra, et cetera, with the 72nd Special Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just part of the 72nd Special Brigade, and that's what written here, and part of my unit and part of Combat Group 3, not Brigade 3. But these were very small units. I think, and I have it written down somewhere, that only two rifle platoons took part because I could not allocate more resources for that. As for "ciscenje," it means separating something good from something bad. If you're asking about this particular case --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Separating something good from something bad? Is that its dictionary definition? We can always find a dictionary definition for it, but separating something good from something bad. It's very familiar to us. Is that really what the word means or have you been discussing evidence with someone else? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, Mr. Nice, am trying to explain to you in the simplest possible way the meaning of a particular word in the Serbian language. And I think that in the English language also this word is used when you're cleaning something. Basically -- well, I don't know how else I can explain this to you. In military terminology, we used this expression only in the sense of fighting against armed terrorists, if that's what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the witness did offer that meaning, that explanation, earlier today, separating something good from something bad. This is not the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, are you referring to "ciscenje" or "ocistila"? Do they have the same meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over here "ocistila," cleaned, that's what it means, that the terrain was searched, the broader area of the village of Rogovo. You will notice that on the 24th the terrorists appeared in the area of Pnis, and that is this entire area on the right bank of the Beli Drim river where the terrorists were quite active, and also further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just please answer the question put to you. I was asking you whether "ocistila" have the same meaning as "ciscenje," and you answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Ocistila" is a noun from the verb "ciscenje," isn't it? "Ciscenje" is a verbal noun, apparently, but they're all the same root, I think. So, look --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the other way around, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You got your Serbian grammar all wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's because you haven't answered the question. If you would just answer the question, then we'd all be wiser instead of leaving it to Mr. Nice to try and clarify the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Ciscenje" and "ocistili" and "ocistilo" and "ocistijo," all of that are verbs. Some are finite and others infinite. Serbian grammar is terribly complicated. I cannot begin to explain this to you over such a short period of time. So this is precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- one of the most complicated grammars, the Serbian grammars. Also Croatian grammar and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what we want you to do is try to tell us the truth, if you wouldn't mind. And what it comes to is this: That in your own hand you use a word from the same root, cleanse, cleaning, that you said your deputy used effectively in error not so many minutes or half hours ago, and yet we find you using the same word yourself. Because cleansing means cleansing, doesn't it? It means taking people out, killing them, and booting them out of the country, and it's a nasty word and that's what you wrote down.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what it means. That is your interpretation. And now why is this unusual for you that two persons from the same country, from the same state, who went to the same schools, use the same word? I mean, it's the same kind of word, like "good day," "good-bye," whatever. Now what is so unusual about that? This term pertains exclusively to fighting against terrorists. I'm repeating that to you yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The number of times you repeat something may or may not add to its validity and strength, but just cast your mind back, Mr. Vukovic, to the opening questions I asked you yesterday, which I intentionally and expressly asked you to use your own terminology to describe what you were doing in this area. Do you remember? Do you remember that passage of questioning? You tried to give a long answer and I brought you back and I fed you back your own words and asked you for any other words that were relevant. I was giving you every opportunity, quite intentionally, to use the word "ciscenje" or one of its family derivatives, and you never did so because you'd forgotten what you'd written down in your own hand. You are a liar, Mr. Vukovic, and this book reveals it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're a liar, Mr. Nice, and I know exactly what I said. If I were to use all the words from military terminology, I would take at least ten days of the Trial Chamber's time. I did not talk about anti-aircraft defence and fighting against landing forces and many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not permissible to describe the Prosecutor as a liar. When he says you are a liar, he does so on the basis of the evidence and his instructions. But you're not permitted to describe him as a liar. You may say that he has wrong information, but don't call him a liar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, would we now read on, because we're going to come to the one passage of this diary that was led through you by the accused. Can we go to the immediately following passage, "ostatak jedinice ..." there, that bit there. Can you start it off and can you read it to us.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The remainder of the unit carried out tasks as planned on the in-depth security of the state border." Next bullet: "During the course of the day, in the direction of the border crossing Cafa Prusit, about 2.000 people crossed over. The transport of children and elderly people was organised." That is what it says in this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on. Let's go on. Next page.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to read on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please read on to the end of this entry.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Djakovica-Prizren road was crowded with columns of refugees. There is nothing sadder than watching a column of poor people who are moving from their homes on someone's instructions. Soldiers are the way they are; they give juice and cookies to children in passing."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two questions arise from that passage. First, transport was organised to take some of these people not to Mother Serbia, not to a safe and secure part of Kosovo which would be under Serbian control, such as, for example, the village of Hoca - yes, Hoca was a village under Serbian control - but to take them to Albania. Why?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, all villages were, if that's the word you use, under Serb control where there were no terrorists. Secondly, they could have gone wherever they wanted to go. And I'm going to give you specific examples by name of persons who went to Mother Serbia, as you put it. Those who wanted to go there, went there. Those who wanted to go to Montenegro, went to Montenegro; and those who didn't want to go to either place went to Albania. And I have spoken extensively about why most of them went to Albania and Macedonia. In order to portray an alleged humanitarian catastrophe to the world and to justify the NATO aggression against my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Let's see if I understand this. I mean, these people who have had their houses burnt out, who have seen their family members killed, are now engaged in a conspiracy of some kind, is it, because they want to portray a humanitarian catastrophe. Who orchestrated this wonderful conspiracy, Mr. Vukovic? Who was there on the ground, saying do this, do that, and we'll make it look as though we're suffering. Who did it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the first, it wasn't people from the area that you are alluding to, to Bela Crkva, Celine, whatever. These people who were passing through the area of defence of my battalion and who were going to the Cafa Prusit border crossing were from Pec, as far as I can remember. Further on, no transport was organised. It was transportation. It was moving people from one place to the other. It's a completely different word. It means a completely different thing. Elderly, children being --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're doing what you accepted is the best way of reconstructing events, because you agreed with me that contemporaneous documents are the best source. This is not only contemporaneous, it's in your hand. You wrote down transport and/or transportation was organised. Please tell the learned Judges what you meant. You wrote it. You tell us. And where was the destination?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. You have managed to confuse even me. What it says is not "transport was organised" but "transportation was organised." Vehicles were organised. Only from the command post in Zub until the Cafa Prusit border crossing. That's one or two kilometres. And it was organised exclusively for old and infirm persons who were left behind by their own families at my command post because they couldn't continue to walk. Cafa Prusit border crossing could only be crossed on foot. I have already explained that it was ready for demolition, that there were minefields on the left- and right-hand sides of the road and that the road itself on the border crossing itself had obstacles put up, anti-armour obstacles, and only one vehicle was able to pass through at a time. And it was done on the 29th and maybe on the 2nd or the 4th perhaps. Right. The 4th of April. Transportation of children and elderly people was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The destination was Albania, as that's the Cafa Prusit crossing. Next question, very simple question: Who organised it?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I organised the transportation for elderly people and children. The groups were not larger than 30. Even if they had been 300, I would have done the same, because they simply didn't have any strength left in them to go on, and they were also unwilling to accept any of the options that I had offered them, and I talked about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... trucks or buses?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One single truck. I did not have buses in my unit. Where would I take buses from? Not a single unit except for the transportation unit has buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, because we've got your words to go on, the children and the elderly seems to exclude the parents. What were you doing transporting children on their own without their parents, making sure they moved that much faster?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I didn't say -- I didn't say they were children without parents. It goes without saying, Mr. Nice, that when you have a year-old baby, it is carried by the mother. But if you know what Siptar families are like and their lifestyle, you would know that they have many children in one family. So there were perhaps a number of women with children and old, infirm persons who couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in your transportation plans, Mr. Vukovic, is there?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is not a detailed report about that activity. I keep trying to tell you that only the most important events of the day I recorded in the war diary. It would have been 10.000 pages long if I had entered details about those people and all the rest. We never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
